Much of the economic data we use to understand the world, such as the incomes people receive, is recorded in the local currencies of each country. On their own, numbers in local currencies tell us nothing about how they compare. One obvious approach would be to convert them into a common currency using market exchange rates. But this doesn’t give us the comparison we often look for: what money can actually buy in different countries. This is because the cost of living varies a lot across countries.

International dollars are a hypothetical currency that aims to have the same purchasing power everywhere. They are adjusted for differences in living costs across countries and price changes over time. Wherever it is “spent”, one international dollar buys the same goods and services as one US dollar would in the United States.

Making incomes comparable across countries matters especially for our understanding of global inequality. Using market dollars — local currencies converted to US dollars using market exchange rates — to compare incomes across countries understates people’s real income in countries where local prices are often much lower than in the US.

Take India, for example. Its gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is almost 30 times lower than that of the US in market dollars. But when we adjust for differences in living costs, the gap shrinks to about eight times lower. For Burkina Faso, the difference is even starker: its GDP per capita is 83 times lower than that of the US in market dollars, and 30 times lower after adjusting for differences in living costs. Global inequality remains large, even after accounting for what people can buy locally.

🚨 BIG NEWS: $NBIS NEBIUS IMPROVES AI TRAINING THROUGHPUT ON 192 NVIDIA B300 GPUs WITHOUT ADDING A SINGLE GPU.

This is a pretty bug technical update from Nebius.

Nebius tested NUMA-aware process affinity on a DeepSeek V3 pretraining workload running across 192 NVIDIA B300 GPUs using Megatron Bridge on its managed Kubernetes platform.

The results? Mean training step time decreased by 1.11%, while model throughput per GPU increased by 1.13%.

Now, 1.13% might not sound impressive initially. But when you're operating thousands of expensive GPUs, even a small improvement in utilization can have meaningful economic value.

Modern GPU servers have multiple CPU sockets and NUMA domains. Each CPU has faster access to its local memory and PCIe connected devices. When training processes get scheduled across the wrong NUMA domains, they can introduce unnecessary memory traffic, latency and communication overhead.

Nebius tested exclusive NUMA binding, which keeps processes closer to their local CPU, memory and GPU resources.

The important part is that they're improving performance through infrastructure level optimization rather than buying additional compute.

Imagine a hypothetical 100,000 GPU deployment achieving the same 1.13% throughput improvement. That's roughly the training throughput equivalent of adding 1,130 GPUs, assuming the improvement scales consistently.

Of course, this benchmark doesn't prove the same gains will hold across every model, cluster or workload.

Nebius is operating in a market where GPUs are extremely expensive, power availability is constrained and customers care about how quickly they can train models.

If Nebius can consistently extract more useful compute from the same hardware, customers can finish training workloads faster while Nebius potentially improves the competitiveness and economics of its cloud platform.

This wasn't a synthetic GPU benchmark. Nebius used a DeepSeek V3 pretraining workload with Megatron Bridge, which makes the result more relevant to actual large model training.

This is what separates simply renting NVIDIA GPUs from building a serious AI cloud platform.

Anybody with enough capital can purchase GPUs. Getting those GPUs to operate efficiently across CPU topology, memory, networking, containers and distributed training software is an entirely different engineering problem.

Nebius is showing that it's paying attention to that layer and as its GPU infrastructure scales, these seemingly small optimizations could become increasingly important to its customers and its own infrastructure economics.

INFLEQTION SAYS IT WILL HAVE A TRULY USEFUL QUANTUM COMPUTER BY 2028

Quantum computers are built from qubits. Most qubits make a lot of mistakes. To fix that, companies group several of them together into one reliable "logical qubit." Logical qubits are the ones that actually matter.

Infleqtion just built 30 logical qubits using only 80 regular ones, per Forbes. Most approaches need far more raw qubits to get there.

Its goal is 100 logical qubits by 2028. That's around the point where quantum computers could start solving problems no regular computer can.

The trick is how it builds them. Infleqtion uses individual atoms held in place by lasers, and every atom can talk to every other atom. Most big players use superconducting chips that need giant freezers and can only connect neighbors.

Those chips are faster, but they need way more steps to do the same work. CTO Pranav Gokhale says that shrinks their speed edge from about 1,000x to about 10x.

"What really matters is if we get to 100 logical qubits near-term as planned. I think that will be a challenge for superconducting systems."

It's already making money too, selling ultra-precise atomic clocks and sensors. It raised more than $500M in its IPO this year and expects about $45M in revenue in 2026.

Population aging is pushing up Chile’s crude cancer death rate, even as age-adjusted rates are falling.

In Chile, the annual number of cancer deaths as a share of the total population has been rising for decades. From this, it would be easy to assume that cancer is getting worse. But the chances of dying from cancer at most ages are lower than they used to be. The missing piece is that the country’s population is changing quickly, and older people now make up a much larger share.

That’s what the chart shows. The crude cancer death rate, in red, counts registered cancer deaths per 100,000 people of all ages. This metric has been going up, reflecting the fact that cancer risks increase steeply with age, and the population has grown much older.

The blue line, by contrast, shows the age-adjusted rate. This metric removes the effect of aging by holding the age structure constant.

This line has been falling for decades, which means that Chileans at almost every age are now less likely to die from cancer than people of the same age were in the past.

The pattern we see in Chile is happening in many other countries, too, and is visible in the global estimates.

(written by @EOrtizOspina)

@primus_labs eliminates this dilemma by deploying a zero-knowledge Proof of Reserves architecture that decouples mathematical solvency verification from data exposure

Verifying asset balances is only one side of the equation; liabilities and total reserve ratios must also be computed confidentially:
 › Blind Balance Computation: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (zkFHE) calculates total assets versus total liabilities across encrypted data states.

Traditional PoR relies on periodic, manual snapshots that fail to prevent flash-loan manipulations between audit windows:

→ Kioxia: trotz kurzfristig schwächerer Guidance bleibt der strukturelle NAND-Treiber Datacenter klar intakt.

→ Sandisk $SNDK: erwartet, dass Datacenter 2027 bereits mehr als 55 % der NAND-Bit-Nachfrage ausmachen.

Das ist nicht das Bild eines AI-Zyklus, der kollabiert.

Ein echter Bust würde typischerweise so aussehen:

Stornierungen → schwächere Auslastung → fallende Preise → sinkende Backlogs → CapEx-Kürzungen

Was wir aktuell sehen, ist fast das Gegenteil:

mehr Orders → steigende Backlogs → knappe Kapazitäten → höhere CapEx-Pläne → Kunden sichern sich Supply Jahre im Voraus

💡 Genau darin liegt für mich der zentrale Disconnect.

Die Unternehmensdaten sagen weiterhin klar:

Compute ist knapp.

Cloud wächst.

Memory bleibt eng.

Networking wird zum nächsten Bottleneck.

Power und genehmigte Datacenter-Kapazität bleiben knapp.

Equipment-Supplier planen bis 2029/30.

Natürlich werden nicht alle AI-Unternehmen gewinnen.

Natürlich wird Kapital zerstört werden.

Und natürlich kann der Markt kurzfristig weiter fallen.

Aber die These, dass AI-Nachfrage gerade einbricht, wird von den operativen Zahlen aktuell nicht bestätigt.

Der Markt hat AI-Risiko deutlich neu bewertet. Die AI-Nachfrage selbst bislang nicht.

Deal economics in AI infrastructure are improving for the landlord.

Two recent Frontier AI Lab comps show the shift:

WULF (Anthropic, 401 MW):

20-year term, $19B contracted ($2.37M revenue per MW/year). More traditional campus build — landlord delivers a higher level of finished infrastructure. CapEx $10–12M/MW. 85% NOI margin. 18% yield on cost.

RIOT (Corsicana, 910 MW):

15-year triple-net powered land lease, $28B contracted ($2.0M revenue per MW/year). Landlord delivers land, power infrastructure, and powered pads. Tenant brings the GPUs (same as WULF) and pays nearly all operating costs. CapEx only $6M/MW. 99% NOI margin. 33% unlevered yield on cost.

Same class of tenant. Similar revenue per MW. The difference is how much of the build the landlord has to fund. The newer structure is more capital-efficient and higher-margin.

This is the trend: as power becomes the scarce asset, landlords who control it can negotiate lighter CapEx and higher-margin structures instead of carrying full facility builds.

$KEEL already has the power secured and is still in active negotiations. No pressure to sign the first deal that shows up — they have the cash to wait for the best structure and terms. While others race to lock something in, $KEEL can let the comps keep improving and take the higher-quality version of the same deal. The first signature will re-rate the entire company, and they get to pick the one that maximizes it.
